title: Graphics in Godot
author: DonCashless
selftext:
I always see really awesome games created with Three.js, but when I try to do the same thing in Godot, pretty much nothing looks really good. It works, but it doesn't look good - whether it's in 3D or with a pixel art style.

What are your best-practice tips for Godot or, more generally, for game engines other than Three.js?

comments.author: Fizassist1
comments.body:
Oh boy.  I've been working in Godot on two separate projects and its been wonderful.  First engine for me, so its a lot to learn but making great progress. 

One thing I do to try to maintain consistency is making my assets in asprite, and never scaling them in Godot.  That way, I've been able to achieve roughly even pixel density.  

Typically ill use chatgpt or some other AI to generate a bubbly cartoon of whatever I need (microscope earlier).  Then import that into aseprite and reduce down to the desired size (nearest neighbor is what I use).  

Also try to keep a size reference sheet if you can.  I base everything off the pixel height of my character sprite.  

Aseprite also has some good tools for despeckling.  I actually recommend using that first before reducing the size, as it seems to make things blend better when its reduced.  

If you put something in your scene that isnt the right size, dont resize in Godot, do it in aseprite.

replies.author: DonCashless
replies.body: Awesome! I will give it a try. Do you control Aseprite via AI or do you control it manually?

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body: yes. aseprite does have an ai plug in but I cant remember what its called and I haven't had the best success with it.  but you could absolutely try it and see what you get!

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
As someone who's built their career making games the old fashioned way, this is how you do it. You need a consistent asset pipeline that produces consistent outputs at consistent scales and sizes before it ever hits the engine. Likewise you should strive to keep your assets in a similar art style if you aren't already. If they look bad together outside of the engine they'll look bad in the engine. If you got that covered then everything gets a _lot_ easier. If something looks wonky don't try to fix it in-engine, fix it at the source.

I'll also add that you're going to have to do some post processing and tweaking once you get things in the engine. Materials, lighting, post processing, all those pieces need to be setup right to get a consistent look and feel.

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body: Thats incredibly motivating to hear from a career professional.  I started Godot 6 months ago and now working on a passion project that can help escape my teaching career.  I teach all levels of high school physics, and have been for 10 years.  But due to budget and standards, my position was eliminated and im forced to teach environmental science at a different school within the district next year.  So, Im currently saving my sanity by building an education game focused on physics, where students build there own lab they can customize via cosmetics earned from mini games and activities.  Literally 36 hours into that one and I've already got a good working framework.  Godot is very fun once you start getting to know the different node types and what they can do.

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body: That's the kinda thing that makes me excited for AI in game dev. The time sink without AI assistance is brutal, even if you do know what you're doing. I want to see what people create when the cost flips and it's easy to make things that look good and play well without spending a decade getting to that point (It was worth every year, but I got lucky). Plus being an engineer, I'm secretly happy I don't have to only stick to capsules and cubes in my demos lol.

replies.author: DonCashless
replies.body: When we talk about AI game development, the question is: Do you provide the pipeline with sample images, a color palette, precise specifications for size, etc., or how do you set up a suitable pipeline?

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
That one I honestly have no idea. Asset generation is something I've been punting entirely till I finish my engine's editor and can start experimenting with things in my own asset pipeline. The most I've done so far is have it generate a cornell box as procedural meshes and had it setup some test scenes.

Though if it's anything like all my other AI usage, you'll probably get the best results with concrete examples and a spec or sketch of what you want. Then give the AI a way to see what it's doing and iterate on it's own rapidly, particularly with some kind of code interface to whatever program you're using. That process gets me very good results on everything I've thrown AI at.

replies.author: silly_bet_3454
replies.body:
You're still missing the point, the assets, the stuff you ultimately see in the game, are independent of the engine. You can take your same assets and put them in 3 or in godot and they will look identical. You can have AI do whatever it's gonna do, the result is still the same in either engine. Godot might have some lighting or other minutia that slightly changes that but not too much.

I think what you're actually observing is just some kind of bias around the kinds of games and styles people gravitate to when using each respective engine.
